Before you commit Whose dividing fence is it, and who pays for what If the fence sits on the boundary it is a dividing fence, and Queensland has a process for sharing the cost. Under the Neighbourhood Disputes (Dividing Fences and Trees) Act 2011, adjoining owners generally contribute equally to a sufficient dividing fence - for residential land that means roughly 0.5 m to 1.8 m high, substantially of prescribed materials such as palings, chain wire, metal panels or brick. If you want more than that, the difference is on you, which is the part that surprises people upgrading to a taller Colorbond run. Talking to your neighbour first, with a written quote in hand, resolves most of these. Where it does not, a notice to contribute is the formal step: an approved form naming the land, the fence line, the work and the estimated cost, with at least one written quotation attached. If there is no agreement within one month, either owner can apply to QCAT within two months of the notice. We can invoice each owner their own share so nobody is chasing the other for money. What nobody can promise you is the outcome, and any site that tells you your neighbour must pay half of a premium fence is guessing. General information as at July 2026. The current rules are published by the Queensland Government and dividing-fence disputes are heard by QCAT . Height, corners and pool barriers Up to 2 m above natural ground level a fence is generally accepted development in Queensland. Above 2 m it becomes building work and needs approval from a certifier. A fence sitting on a retaining wall is measured as the combined height, so a modest wall plus a standard fence can cross the 2 m line without anyone intending it to. Corner blocks have sight-line truncations at the intersection, so front fencing there is kept low enough for drivers to see across.
